clinicalScope: Genetic code in human protein synthesis for clinicians in low‑resource settings
title: Genetic Code
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: The genetic code translates mRNA codons into amino acids during protein synthesis. Clinicians need to understand its degeneracy, wobble rules, and how mutations alter codons, affecting disease and drug response.

sections.p: The genetic code is the set of rules by which three‑nucleotide codons in mRNA specify the 20 standard amino acids and stop signals. It is nearly universal, with only a few organelle‑specific variations.
During translation, ribosomes read mRNA codons, tRNAs bring matching amino acids, and peptide bonds form a polypeptide chain. The code is degenerate: multiple codons encode the same amino acid.

t.b: If anticodon matches codon, amino acid is added

sections.p: The genetic code is fixed, but expression is regulated by promoter strength, mRNA stability, and translational efficiency. Wobble pairing allows flexibility at the third codon position.
Point mutations can change codons to encode different amino acids (missense), introduce stop codons (nonsense), or delete codons (frameshift). These alter protein function and can cause disease.
Understanding codon changes helps interpret genetic tests, predict drug metabolism (e.g., CYP450 variants), and explain phenotypes of inherited disorders.
Remember the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). Degeneracy means 61 codons for 20 amino acids. Wobble allows G‑U pairing at third position.

faq.q: What is the difference between a missense and a nonsense mutation?
faq.a: Missense changes one amino acid; nonsense introduces a stop codon, truncating the protein.

faq.q: Why is the genetic code called degenerate?
faq.a: Because multiple codons encode the same amino acid, providing redundancy.

faq.q: How does wobble pairing affect translation?
faq.a: It allows tRNAs to pair with multiple codons at the third position, increasing translational efficiency.

exam: A patient with a known pathogenic missense mutation in the CFTR gene – what is the likely effect on protein function? — Loss of chloride channel activity, leading to viscous secretions.
In a pharmacogenomic panel, a patient has a UTR variant that reduces mRNA stability – how does this affect drug dosing? — Lower protein levels, may require higher dose or alternative drug.
During translation, a tRNA with a G‑U wobble pair binds a codon – what does this demonstrate? — Wobble base‑pairing allows flexibility at the third codon position.
A newborn shows a premature stop codon in the β‑globin gene – what disease is likely? — β‑thalassemia major.
A patient presents with a frameshift mutation in the dystrophin gene – what clinical feature would you expect? — Progressive muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy.
A genetic test shows a synonymous codon change in a tumor suppressor gene – what is the clinical significance? — Usually benign, but may affect splicing or translation efficiency.
